# Get started on Zephyr native_sim

<!-- type: how-to · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [Install](../start/install.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: starter status -->
> **Status:** Verified on host (merge). From the board support registry: [`nros-board-zephyr`](../reference/boards/zephyr-native-sim.md); [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words.
<!-- END GENERATED starter status -->

This starter puts a talker on Zephyr 3.7's `native_sim` board, which builds a
Zephyr application as an ordinary program for your Linux machine, and shows
its messages arriving in ROS 2. There is no emulator: the Zephyr kernel runs
inside one host process, and its sockets are your host's, so the talker
reaches a router on this machine with no network setup. nano-ros is a Zephyr
module here: `nros run` writes the Zephyr application for your image and
builds it with Zephyr's `west`. You write the talker in Rust or in C; pick a
tab and every tab on the page follows.

## What you need

- A Linux x86_64 host with the [install](../start/install.md) done, so `nros`
  is on your `PATH`.
- ROS 2 Humble with `ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp`. ROS 2 provides the zenoh
  router the talker talks to, and the message definitions the build
  generates the talker's code from.
- Zephyr's host tools: `west` and the build tools
  [Zephyr's Getting Started](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/3.7.0/develop/getting_started/index.html)
  lists. `nros setup` installs no system packages, so install them yourself.
  On Debian or Ubuntu:

```bash probe=30
sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git cmake ninja-build gperf \
    device-tree-compiler python3-pip python3-venv xz-utils file wget
pip3 install --user west
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

No board, no cable and no root access: the board's own configuration routes
the application's sockets to the host's, so no TAP interface is created.

## Provision

Provision the board:

```bash probe=32
nros setup zephyr --rmw zenoh
export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR="$(nros locate tool zephyr-sdk)"
```

That fetches the Zephyr SDK and the zenoh-pico and mbedtls sources into a
shared store under `~/.nros`. It installs no router: the router is ROS's
`rmw_zenohd`.

Zephyr's sources live in a west workspace of your own. This one pins Zephyr
3.7 and fetches only the modules nano-ros's boards build with (`import: true`
would fetch every vendor's HAL, about 2.5 GB more), plus Zephyr's Rust
support, which only a Rust talker builds with:

```bash probe=34
mkdir -p my_zephyr_ws/manifest && cd my_zephyr_ws
cat > manifest/west.yml <<'WEST_YML'
manifest:
  remotes:
    - name: zephyrproject-rtos
      url-base: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos
  projects:
    - name: zephyr
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: v3.7.0
      import:
        name-allowlist: [cmsis, picolibc, mbedtls, tinycrypt, mcuboot, net-tools]
    # Rust support: only a Rust app builds with it. Pinned to the revision
    # nano-ros's own west.yml pins for the 3.7 line (it has no release tags).
    - name: zephyr-lang-rust
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: 404fcefdbab0f2711cd342a1fab9d2eda52a1ba9
      path: modules/lang/rust
  self:
    path: manifest
WEST_YML
west init -l manifest
west update --narrow -o=--depth=1
pip3 install --user -r zephyr/scripts/requirements-base.txt
export ZEPHYR_BASE="$PWD/zephyr"
```

## Scaffold the project

Scaffold the workspace beside the west workspace, and tell `nros` where the
west workspace is with `NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE`:

<!-- tabs -->

### Rust

```bash probe=40
. "$HOME/.cargo/env"
export NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE="$PWD"
cd ..
nros new zs_ws --board zephyr --template talker --lang rust --rmw zenoh
cd zs_ws
nros setup --sudo
```

A Rust application on Zephyr needs three things a C one does not: the Rust
target the board implies (`x86_64-unknown-none` for `native_sim/64` on an
x86_64 host), rustup's `clippy` (Zephyr's Rust support lints every Rust app
as it builds), and clang with libclang, for the bindings it generates from
Zephyr's headers. `nros setup` in the workspace installs the target and
`clippy`, and with `--sudo` the two packages. Without `--sudo` it prints the
install command instead.

### C

```bash probe=40
export NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE="$PWD"
cd ..
nros new zs_ws --board zephyr --template talker --lang c --rmw zenoh
cd zs_ws
```

<!-- /tabs -->

That wrote a workspace with two packages: `src/zs_node/`, the talker, a
library with no `main()` that names no board, and `src/zs_node_bringup/`,
whose `system.toml` holds one image, `[image.zephyr]`, with
`board = "zephyr"`: Zephyr's `native_sim/native/64`. The Zephyr application
itself is generated under `build/` when you build, so you write no
`CMakeLists.txt` and no `prj.conf`.

## Run it on this machine

Source ROS 2, then build and run. This first run records the ROS 2 prefix in
the workspace, so later runs of it need no sourced shell (the router still
comes from ROS 2):

```bash probe=50 probe-run=1500
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run zs_node --expect 'Publishing:'
```

```text probe-expect=50
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after
```

The image dials a router on this machine's port 7447, so `nros run` starts
that router, ROS's `rmw_zenohd`, then builds the application through west
(the first build takes several minutes; later ones take seconds) and runs
`zephyr.exe`. Don't start a router of your own on the same port. With
`--expect` it stops everything and exits 0 at the first line containing that
text, and exits 1 if the application stops first.

Without `--expect` it keeps running until you press Ctrl-C, which stops the
application and the router together. Start it that way in one terminal:

```bash probe=60 probe-run=120 probe-keep
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run zs_node
```

```text probe-expect=60
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
```

## See it in ROS 2

Leave `nros run` going. In a second terminal:

```bash probe=70 probe-run=120
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort
```

```text probe-expect=70
data: 'Hello World:
```

The talker publishes best-effort, and `ros2 topic echo` defaults to reliable,
which receives nothing from it. That is why the command asks for best-effort.

## If it doesn't work

- **`eth_posix: Cannot create zeth` on the console:** the application tried
  to create a TAP interface instead of using the host's sockets. The board's
  configuration prevents that; an application you configured yourself needs
  nano-ros's `nros-nsos` snippet.
- **`nros run` refuses a Rust image and names `clang`, `clippy` or the Rust
  target:** run `nros setup --sudo` in the workspace again, or the install
  command it prints.
- **`nros run` stops at once and names the router:** it could not find
  `rmw_zenohd`, or another router already holds port 7447.
- **Everything else:** [Troubleshooting - First 10 Minutes](../reference/troubleshooting-index.md).
